message.content:
You are black-box reverse-engineering a compiled C++ binary. You MUST NOT look for or read any C++ library source (there is none on disk; `idna.hpp` does not exist). Derive behavior ONLY by running the binary.

BINARY: /workspace/dataset/test4_executable
Invoke as: /workspace/dataset/test4_executable "<domain-string>"
It prints exactly 4 lines, each "1" or "0", in this order:
  line1 = idna::is_valid_domain(input)
  line2 = idna::is_valid_label(input)
  line3 = idna::is_ascii_domain(input)
  line4 = idna::is_idn_domain(input)
With no argument, input defaults to the literal string "example.com".

ENVIRONMENT NOTES (important):
- python3 / python are NOT installed. perl may not be installed.
- Use bash loops, printf, tr, head, sed, awk to build test strings.
- Handy helper you can paste:
    rep() { local n=$1 c=$2 s=""; for ((i=0;i<n;i++)); do s+="$c"; done; printf '%s' "$s"; }
  or:  s=$(head -c 64 /dev/zero | tr '\0' 'a')
- To emit arbitrary/high bytes use: printf '\xNN'  (bash $'...' quoting also works)
- rustc and cargo ARE available if you need a quick generator program.

ALREADY-ESTABLISHED FACTS (verify, do not blindly trust):
- "" (empty)        -> 0 0 1 0
- "example.com"     -> 1 1 1 0
- "例子.测试"        -> 1 1 0 1
- "a"x63            -> 1 1 1 0
- "a"x64            -> 1 0 1 0   (is_valid_label flips off above 63)
- "a"x255           -> 1 0 1 0
- "a"x256           -> 0 0 1 0   (is_valid_domain flips off above 255)
- "." ".." "a." ".a" "a..b" "-a.com" "a-.com" "a_b.com" "a b.com" "a/b.com" "*.com" -> all 1 1 1 0

Be rigorous and quantitative. Bisect every boundary you claim (test N-1, N, N+1). Report exact reproducible command lines as evidence.


ADVERSARIAL VERIFICATION TASK.
Another agent studied the dimension "cli-and-output" and proposes this rule about the binary:

  RULE: All output goes to stdout; stderr is always empty (0 bytes) in every case tested.
  Their claimed evidence: $ cd /workspace/dataset
$ ./test4_executable example.com 1>/dev/null 2>&1 | od -c
0000000                    # nothing on stderr
$ ./test4_executable example.com 1>/dev/null 2>/tmp/err.txt; wc -c </tmp/err.txt
0
$ ./test4_executable 2>/tmp/e1 >/dev/null; ./test4_executable "" 2>/tmp/e2 >/dev/null; ./test4_executable --help 2>/tmp/e3 >/dev/null; ./test4_executable a b c 2>/tmp/e4 >/dev/null; wc -c /tmp/e1 /tmp/e2 /tmp/e3 /tmp/e4
0 /tmp/e1
0 /tmp/e2
0 /tmp/e3
0 /tmp/e4
0 total

Your job is to REFUTE it. Actively hunt for a counterexample by running /workspace/dataset/test4_executable yourself. Do not take their evidence on faith — re-run it. Then attack:
 - boundary off-by-ones (test N-1, N, N+1 around every number in the rule)
 - bytes vs codepoints confusion if the rule mentions a length
 - non-ASCII / invalid-UTF-8 inputs
 - empty string and single-character inputs
 - whether the rule over-generalizes from a small sample

Set holds=false and give the exact counterexample input + observed 4-line output if you find one. If the rule is directionally right but imprecise, set holds=false and put a precise version in correctedStatement. Only set holds=true if you genuinely tried and failed to break it. Default to skepticism.

- deep-research: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. - When the user wants a deep, multi-source, fact-checked research report on any topic. BEFORE invoking, check if the question is specific enough to research directly — if underspecified (e.g., "what car to buy" without budget/use-case/region), ask 2-3 clarifying questions to narrow scope. Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

The BINARY ITSELF never writes to stderr - this is true by construction, not just by sampling - but the rule as stated is over-general in three ways.

WHAT IS TRUE (and provable, stronger than what they claimed): the program's only output sink is std::cout. `nm -u /workspace/dataset/test4_executable` imports `_ZSt4cout` and has NO `_ZSt4cerr`, no `stderr`, and no `fprintf`/`fputs`/`puts`/`write` import. main (0x402360-0x402450) performs exactly 4x `std::ostream::_M_insert<bool>` on the std::cout object at 0x4081c0, each followed by `std::endl` (which flushes), then returns 0. So stdout is always exactly 8 bytes ("1"/"0" + "\n", x4) and exit code is always 0 whenever the process actually runs. Further, the four functions main calls (is_valid_domain 0x40277a, is_valid_label 0x4027bb, is_ascii_domain 0x4027fa, is_idn_domain 0x402879) only call empty()/length()/begin()/end()/operator*/operator++ - they perform no allocation and contain no throw site, so the libstdc++ verbose terminate handler (the only in-process code that could reach fd 2) is unreachable from ANY input. The binary does import `__cxa_rethrow`, `__throw_length_error`, `__throw_bad_alloc` and `std::string::reserve`, but only inside functions main never calls (split_labels, to_ascii, punycode_*, etc.), so those throw paths are dead for this CLI.

WHAT IS WRONG / IMPRECISE:
1. "stderr is always empty" is false for the documented invocation form. At argument length >= 131072 bytes the invocation `/workspace/dataset/test4_executable "<string>"` yields rc=126 (or 127), 0 bytes on stdout, and 79 bytes on stderr ("Argument list too long"). Sharp boundary: 131071 bytes works, 131072 fails. Similarly under `ulimit -v <= 4096` the dynamic loader writes 127-132 bytes to stderr with rc=127. In both cases the failure is in the exec/loader layer and the binary never runs - so the honest statement is about the process, not the command line.
2. "All output goes to stdout" must not be read as "the 4 lines always appear on stdout". With stdout a pipe whose reader closes, the process dies on SIGPIPE (rc=141) having delivered 0 bytes; with stdout `>/dev/full` or closed (`>&-`) it exits rc=0 having written nothing and reporting nothing. The program never checks or reports write errors.
3. Their sample was 5 invocations. I ran ~1,400 with zero stderr bytes and stdout always exactly 8 bytes: all 255 single-byte inputs (0x01-0xFF); 308 two-byte invalid-UTF-8 combinations (lead bytes C0,C1,C2,DF,E0,E1,ED,EE,EF,F0,F1,F4,F5,F7,F8,FB,FC,FD,FE,FF,80,BF x 14 continuations, incl. overlongs, surrogates, 5/6-byte leads); 600 random /dev/urandom strings of 1-40 bytes; 192 structured repeats of `. - _ a xn-- 0xFF 0xC3A9 0xE4BE8B .. .-. A 0 SPACE TAB 0x7F 0x01` at k = 1,2,3,4,62,63,64,253,254,255,256,1000; lengths 1000/10000/50000/100000/131000/131070/131071; 65535 and 131071 consecutive dots; 43690x U+4F8B; 32767x U+10000; 65535x 0xFF; 65535x 0x80. Also clean: LC_ALL=C / en_US.UTF-8 / bogus.INVALID, LC_NUMERIC=tr_TR, MALLOC_CHECK_=3, MALLOC_PERTURB_=165, GLIBCXX_FORCE_NEW=1, LD_BIND_NOW=1, LD_DEBUG=unused, stdin closed (`<&-`), stderr closed (`2>&-`), and argv[0] rewritten via `exec -a WEIRDNAME`.

Two CLI facts the rule omits that are worth recording: main branches on `cmp $0x1,%ebx; jle` (0x402383), i.e. argv[1] is used only when argc >= 2 and argv[2..] are silently ignored ("a b c" -> 1,1,1,0, identical to "a"); and argc == 0 (verified with an execve harness passing an empty argv) falls into the default branch and prints the "example.com" result 1,1,1,0.

PRECISE VERSION: "The process writes only to stdout - exactly 8 bytes, four '1'/'0' lines each terminated by '\n' and flushed via std::endl - and exits 0. It links no stderr writer at all (std::cout only; no std::cerr/stderr/fprintf), and the four functions main invokes are allocation-free and throw-free, so no input can make the process emit anything on stderr. Non-empty stderr with zero stdout is still reachable at the command line, but only from failures outside the process: argument length >= 131072 bytes (execve E2BIG, rc=126/127, 79 bytes of shell diagnostic; 131071 bytes is the last working length) and dynamic-loader failure under ulimit -v <= 4096 (rc=127, 127-132 bytes). Conversely, stdout receiving the 4 lines is not guaranteed: SIGPIPE kills it at rc=141 with 0 bytes delivered, and write failures to /dev/full or a closed fd 1 are silently ignored with rc=0."
